title: Wordsworth House, Main Street, Cockermouth
description:
Wordsworth House is a north country merchant's two storey stone houseo f modest proportions built in 1745. The poet William Wordsworth was obrn here in 1770. The house, acquired by the National Trust in 1938, contains an original staircase, panelling and fire-places. (PD Claris; 1986)
Although Cockermouth is noted throughout the workld as the birthplace of William Wordsworth, surprisingly little is known about hte fine Georgian house where he was born in April 1770. Besides his oft-quoted reminiscences of walking along the terrace at the bottom of the garden, there is surely much archival material concerning the house which still gatheres dust in public (Carlisle Records Office) and Private (Lowther MS) records.
Superficially, the detailing and design of the house fits the known fact (recorded on the sandstone lintel over hte back door) that the house was built in 1746 by the High Sheriff of Cumberland. The facade is topped by a moulded cornice (this and original guttering are carried around the house) and two rows of sash windows are broken at ground floor level by a projecting Tuscan proch. Inside, engaged composite columns flank the entry through from the hall to the stairs. The panelling and plasterwork is typical for a c1730-50 date. The greatest subject of decoration is the Dining Room ceiling on the ground floor, with its large central panel framed by 4 spandrel panels.
The plan form of the 1746 building is somewhat more elusive: two partition walls onthe first floor present problems of their own while the absence of any known invertories of the contents of the house make the task of detecting the original function of these rooms more difficult.
A stable and washhouse lie in a separate building attached to the E gable of Wordsworth's House.
one unusual feature worth mentioning is that there are no back stairs; the only possible site for these would have been rising from the cellars to the bedrooms above.
The garden stretching back towards the Derwent, rises to the terrace at the rear.
THE EARLIER HOUSE - The evidence at present available suggests that the High Sheriff's dwelling was converted from a seventeenth or early eighteenth century gentry house. The evidence for this is summarised below.
PLAN FORM - THe wall that axially divides the house is askew ( i.e. the E line of the wall is not properly aligned to the W line of the wall). There are traces of an earlier ciruit plan for door openings sealed off by panelling in 1746. At ground floor level one can see that this tone wall was cut back to provide a sufficiently wide opening for the door. In one of the bedrooms of the 1st floor, the brick fireplace is asymmetrically placed in the room, thus squeezing the window to the W into a tighter position than that on the E.
BUILDING MATERIALS - On the first floor only the E/W axial wall is continued up at attic level but here it can be seem that some early to mid 18th century bricks were used to complete the triangulation of the inner and outer gable walls and over one bedroom and the dressing room to make a closed truss wall. The main cross walls rise unbroken from the cellars, the W end of which was blocked off in the later 18th cnetury. It seems that the two storey cottage attached to the E gable wall would be of the same date.
CELLAR, STABLE / WASHHOUSE BLOCK and GARDEN DOORS. SASH WINDOWS to N ELEVATION - In the celalrs is one chamfered door architrave, very similar to a door in the garden. These doors, the other doors in the garden, and the twin doors to the two storey cottage in the N elevation, are stylisticaly of early to mid 17th century date.
The garden doors themselves are built into brick walls. The E wall is the most interesting, for it is faced on the E with stone rubble but to the W with 2 1/4" brick (4 courses rise 11 1/2"). The W wall is built of 9" X 4 1/2" X 2 1/2" brick, but for a brick wall of early to mid 17th centuty date one would expect the bricks to be longer and flatter: the only solution to this problem woudl be to project the date of teh door architraves forward to the late 17th or early 18th centuries...
On the N elevation are some 18th century sash windows with huge 2" glazing bars. The windows are set back in shallow reveals and ahve chamfered or ovolo moulded sandstone architraves. They appear to be of a much earlier type than the sash windows along the facade, and the workmanship is of poorer quality (which is to be expected). It is therefore possible that these windows (which could be dated to around 1710-30) belonged to the earlier house.
LATER INSERTIONS
BRICK and LATH and PLASTER WALLS - These lie to the NW on teh first floor.
BRICK WALL - this could well date back to 1746 since these bricks are of the 3" type, wider and shorter than the other 2 1/2" bricks in the attic. The inclusions in the bricks also suggest that the caly was dug from different areas. These bricks do, however, amke up a wall which holds a scarfed tie beam supporting two E facing trusses: the principal rafters of these trusses actually join the tie beam between this wall and the stone wall adjoining the staircase. It is therefore possible that the roof trusses (of king post type with original carpenters' marks) post- date the insertion of this wall.
LATH and PLASTER WALL - It is difficult to date this portion, and indeed opposing arguements can be brought forth to support or refute any suggestion that it could be of a late date.
SUPPORT - The mouldings to the architrave of the door differs from other doors.
The dado rail in the passage formed by the partition is identical to the dado rail in the ground floor back passage. The ground floor dado actually covers a blocked doorway which once led into the cellar under the kitchen.
On the first floor it is probably that a door was inserted in the late 18th century. One door mirrors the postition of the blocked door and so probably dates from the earliest phase of the hosue. One would expect it to lead into a drawing room or bedroom instead of the bottom of a passage. This therefore makes it probable that the partition was a later insertion. IT is, however, possible that this partition was already installed at the time of Wordsworth's birth - local tradition, indeed, has it that this was his birthplace and nursery. THe installation of such a partition would surely not have been beyond the means of the poet's father, John (1741-1783) who was the Agent of Sir Jamer Lowther.
The neo-classical fireplace pediments date back to teh period 1770-80 and probably were inserted at the same time as the partition.
AGAINST - The moulding to the door is the same as that to the inner architraves of the two windows in the room, and with the exception of there being a cyma instead of an ovolo mouldedcentre step is identical to the other window architraves on the first and ground floors of the house. The partition wall is the only wall in the house not carried on below. One could simply argue that because it is nonstructural, and hence lath and plaster, there is no reason why it could not be original.
Late 18th century doors and 6 light horizontal sliding sash window to washhouse.
Victorian double hung sashes with cut back lugs inserted in two windows on ground floor.
CONCLUSION - There are two alternatives.
1) The first phase of building dates to the early 17th century. Dating from this period would be the 3 attic windows, the square headed, pointed and chamfered door architraves above mentioned.
2) The above mentioned phase dates to the early 18th cnetury (i.e. when the sash windows with the wide and crudely mitred glazing bars were fitted). Some doors on both floors would have certainly completed a typically early 18th century circuit plan. Another feature more usually found in early 18th cnetury contexts is the bolechain moulded fireplace on the first floor.
It is probable that the lath and plaster partition ia a later addition, but certainly not post-dating the late 18th century.
FRONT DOOR - tuscan porch; moulded sandstone arhitraves, cyna reversa moulding to edge of field.
BACK DOOR - Sandstone architrave. 6 panelled: ovolo & fillet moulded to raised field.
GROUND FLOOR
DINING / ASSEMBLY ROOM -
CEILING - The moulding sand the layout of the plaster ceiling - central decorative panels - are typical of mid-eighteenth plasterwork ceiligns: the motifs, such as the husk-chains, are typical of a c.1730-50 date.
CORNICE - Ionic; husk pendants between dentils.
FIREPLACE - Ovolo moulded edge to stepped architrave.
COMMON PARLOUR
CORNICE - Doric; rosette ornatment to face to meopes, anil motifs to soffit of mutules, and to soffit of corona between mutules.
PANELLED WALLS - Alcove with shell top.
FIREPLACE - Stepped architrave.
STEWARD / HOUSEKEEPER'S ROOM - Neo classical pediment over original fireplace. Tiled surround to fireplace: mid 18th cnetury handpainted tiles: very pale blue tiles (near to off-white) are painted in light blue brushwork depicting two scenes, a man (dresses like a prince) being lowered on a rope from the parapet of a large house.
FIRST FLOOR - Moulded dado rail to each room.
DRAWING ROOM
CORNICE - Ionic: the soffit of each dentil is decorated with acanthus leaf motifs and between each dentil is a rosette. Scrolled pediments over spposing doors: same treatment as above to dentils. Central earthouche.
PANELLED WALLS - Panelling typical of 1720-50 period; the edges of each panel are ovolo moulded and then cyma moulded to a raised field. (The cyma moulding here bein gmore expensive than the usual flat planed rise to the field.
An elaborate neo-classical cornice surmounts the fireplace.
BEDROOM 1 - Neo-classical pediment over fireplace.
BEDROOM 2 - Fireplace - Stepped architrave
LANDING - Cornice: Ionic entablature, with rosettes between dentils. Plaster ceiling over staircase.
BEDROOM 3 - Elaborate neo-classical cornice over fireplace. Original fireplace has bolechion moulded architrave (early 18th century).
DRESSING ROOM - Art Nouveau (c1910) plasterwork to cornice over picture rail. Stepped architravbe to fireplace.
BEDROOM 4 - Neo-classical cornice over original fireplace: this has stepped architraves with a beaded arris.
Also associated with this house in an Old Coach House now a shop (20240*1) and a toilet block (20240*2).
(NT VBS Surveyor; 1983)

title: Land Adjacent to 18 Wordsworth Avenue, Newham, London: An Archaeological Evaluation Report
description: In May 2019, AOC Archaeology Group conducted an archaeological evaluation at the site known as Land adjacent to 18 Wordsworth Avenue, Newham, London; TQ 42237 84534. The site evaluation was composed of three trenches measuring between 3.50m and 18.00m long by 2.00m wide, located to target areas to be impacted upon by the development as well as give good coverage of the site within the constraints.    The site sequence revealed natural yellow/orange brown sand and gravels overlain with a disturbed sandy gravel subsoil and brickearth in patches. Layers of made ground were observed in all trenches and comprised rubble with CBM, concrete, brick fragments and gravel as well as made ground comprising yellow sand in Trench 3 in the south-east of the site. Structural remains of a post-medieval or modern cellar were encountered as well as evidence for modern drainage and services. All trenches indicated significant horizontal truncation, indicated by the presence of the natural sand and gravels directly overlain by modern made ground deposits.  No further archaeological work is recommended for the site. The archive will be collated and deposited with the London Archaeological Archive Research Centre (LAARC). The results will be published through the Archaeology Data Service website and copies of the report available at the local studies library.

title: CHAD VARAH HOUSE, DRURY LANE / WORDSWORTH STREET, LINCOLN: ARCHAEOLOGICAL MONITORING AND STRIP, MAP AND RECORD REPORT
description: Monitoring of groundwork in Areas 1 -5 only revealed modern make-up and garden soil deposits. Boreholes in Areas 1 and 2 did however encounter archaeological deposits between c 1.4m and 4m - 5m below present ground level, but no firm datable material was collected from any of these deposits which lay significantly below the formation level of the redevelopment.     During the strip, map and record excavations in Area 6, structural remains were encountered, likely forming a structure and associated internal surface. Finds recovered from overlying deposits were of post-medieval date (17th - 18th century), and the structural remains were thereby assigned to the late medieval/post-medieval period. Excavation of a large pit cutting the east/west aligned wall also contained pottery dating to the 18th century, confirming this approximate date for the structure. Excavation of a slot through the structure, removed to allow for a greater understanding of the exposed stonework, including construction and phasing, revealed a buried soil horizon directly below the postulated internal surface of the structure. This buried soil contained pottery dating to the 14th and 15th centuries AD and overlay an earlier north-east to south-west orientated limestone wall; cut into an earlier buried soil from which only Roman pottery was retrieved. This suggests the north-east - south-west wall is also of medieval date (pre-15th century), but with only a small area of the buried soil containing Roman pottery revealed within the slot excavation, a definitive date for that soil horizon (and therefore earliest date for the wall) could not be determined.

title: Extension to Warden's House, Bailgate Court, Wordsworth Street, City of Lincoln: Report on a Scheme of Archaeological Monitoring and Recording
description: The programme of archaeological monitoring and recording initially consisted of the monitoring of a 2.0m x 2.0m trial pit, to be excavated in the centre of the footprint of the proposed building in order to identify the targeted horizon for the base of the six stanchion pits of the raft foundation of the new building, with a second phase of monitoring during the excavation of the stanchion pits. Following the excavation of the trial pit, the methodology was expanded, in consultation with the City Archaeologist, to include the full excavation to the first archaeological horizon of the entire building footprint, which was then to be back-filled under archaeological supervision before the excavation of the stanchion pits. Machine excavation of the test pit and the subsequent extended excavation area was carried out using a tracked mini-digger fitted with a toothless ditching bucket. Overburden and made ground were removed to the first archaeological horizon, and the exposed surfaces were cleaned by hand and recorded in plan and section, in accordance with the approved WSI. The excavated area was then back-filled and consolidated under archaeological supervision, protecting exposed remains with geotextile, before the excavation of the stanchion pits. All deposits and features seen were recorded on standard PCAS context recording sheets, and the progress of the groundworks noted on standard PCAS site diary sheets. Features were cleaned and sample excavated by hand before being drawn in section at scale 1:20. A plan of the excavation area was created using GPS surveying. A digital photographic record was also maintained The west-north-west to east-south-east aligned limestone rubble wall footing exposed in the excavation area can be dated with reasonable certainty to the Roman colonia settlement, and may correspond to remains of other stone buildings discovered during archaeological works at Spring Hill, St. Michael's Terrace and Stanthaket Court, as well as possibly being associated with traces of a north-to-south-aligned road roughly following the line of the north end of Gibraltar Hill. The Lincoln Archaeological Research Agenda notes that the steep slopes of the hillside above the River Witham were probably first settled in the later Roman period (RAZ 7.11.4), and this corresponds to the  mid- to late 2nd century or later pottery retrieved, dating to a period well after the military occupation of Lincoln had ceased at the end of the 1st century AD, but probably before the civilian settlement was fortified in the 3rd century.  The identification of a stone foundation beneath the brick wall of the hospital grounds, possibly indicating the re-use of an earlier boundary, may have a bearing on the Research Agenda note that commercial premises on street-fronting plots in the Lower City gave way to the dwellings of the wealthy during the economically depressed period between the mid-14th and mid-18th centuries (RAZ 10.25). The brick footings of the north-eastern corner of a building, which were exposed at the south side of the excavation area, are likely to have been part of a building shown  in the hospital grounds on the 1868 town plan; no other elements of the hospital grounds were exposed.

title: Dove Cottage, Grasmere, Cumbria: An architectural analysis of Wordsworth's Grasmere home (1799-1808), its origins and evolution
description: Dove Cottage, a Grade I listed building, is internationally famous as the home, between 1799 and 1808, of William and Dorothy Wordsworth, and as the meeting place during their residence of many of the greatest figures of British Romanticism, including Coleridge, Southey, Scott, Wilson and De Quincey. Built as a two-storeyed vernacular house probably in the late 17th century or around 1700, Dove Cottage is constructed of irregular fieldstone rubble with a Cumbrian slate roof. It is built to an irregular plan consisting of a two-bay front range, a single-bay rear range, a small projecting pantry (known to Dorothy Wordsworth as the 'out-jutting') and, at the opposite end of the house, an attached outbuilding, probably intended as a stable. Photographs of the front range, taken when external roughcast was removed in the 1970s, show that it originally incorporated wider, lower windows which must have been mullioned. They were altered to receive taller, narrower casement windows probably in the second quarter of the 18th century, when raised-and-fielded panelling was introduced to the ground-floor rooms of the front range, and several panelled internal doors were introduced. Wordsworth's poem Benjamin the Waggoner is the source for the tradition that the house served as an alehouse (the Dove and Olive Bough) at some point prior to 1799.

title: New Emergency Access for Bishop Wordsworth's School, Salisbury, Wiltshire, Historic Building Record and Archaeological Watching Brief
description: Wessex Archaeology was commissioned by Bell Cornwell on behalf of Bishop Wordsworth's School to carry out a programme of historic building recording and archaeological watching brief on the west boundary wall at Bishop Wordsworth's School, Exeter Street, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 2ED. The wall is a Grade II listed building named 'WALL RUNNING NORTH OF LODGE, PARALLEL WITH ROAD'. The recording occurred prior to and during construction of a new emergency access in March and October 2019 respectively.    The list entry dates the wall to the late 16th century. The lower part of the wall is constructed of a mix of stone rubble, flint and red brick with some occasional tile. Probably in the later 18th or early 19th century the wall was raised, and an opening infilled leaving a narrow pedestrian doorway. The new emergency access reinstates the width of the earlier opening.     There is evidence that indicates the wall terminals of the new emergency access were rebuilt prior to the raising and infilling of the wall, but no earlier than the 18th century. The brick lacing courses to the north of the entrance may indicate that this section of wall was also wholly or substantially rebuilt at this time, perhaps in the earlier part of the 18th century. Conversely, the absence of brick lacing to the south suggests this part of the wall was probably repaired rather than rebuilt and thus largely survives from an earlier, possibly late 16th century date.

title: New Classrooms, Bishop Wordsworth's School Salisbury,Archaeological Watching Brief
description: Wessex Archaeology was commissioned by Bishop Wordsworth's Grammar School (the Client), to undertake an archaeological watching brief during works associated with the construction of a new teaching block at the school. The monitored works covered 0.8 ha, centred on NGR 414461 129495, at Bishop Wordsworth's School, Cathedral Close, Salisbury, Wiltshire, SP1 2EF. Two structures were revealed during the course of the watching brief. Both features were present at relatively shallow depths below the modern hardstanding and made ground deposits and were relatively undisturbed by modern intrusions.     The southernmost of these structures (Structure 1) expanded on a previous investigation which is believed to represent part of the 19th century Bishop's Stables, which were demolished following a fire in 1965. Beneath these was an extensive and thick deposit of made ground containing medieval material, on which the buildings had been constructed. Beneath made ground were extensive deposits of alluvial silt. Structure 2 in the northern part of site consisted of a single wall and associated mortar/gravel spread. Although undated, the wall and deposit appear to follow the ordination of a boundary path shown on 18th and 19th century historical mapping.

title: Rydal Mount Garden and House
description:
House and garden (home of William Wordsworth) of Post Medieval date.

Rydal Mount, C16-18. The home of Wm Wordsworth from 1813 until he died in 1850. 3 storeys, colour-washed stone rubble, slate roof with round chimneys, gabled porch, new windows. Lower wings are 2 storeys. E block late C16. W wing C17. A cross-wing added ca 1700 at N end of original block. A mid C18 block between the original house and the W wing. LB Grade II (S1268). Listed in the National Parks & Gardens Register as Grade II no. 1663. The early C19 garden, c 2ha, created by Wordsworth after moving from the parsonage at Grasmere to Rydal Mount in 1813. The garden contains a vestigial Mound or Mount, probably C16 (S1324). Also see the NAS Gazetteer (S1323). The grounds at Rydal Mount encompass 2 hectacres. The gardens have been described as well-designed and executed by William Wordsworth. There are a series of four garden terraces surrounded by hedges (S3203, p. 227).

title: Dove Cottage at Town End, Grasmere
description:
A 17th-18th century Cottage (a domestic, residential building), once home to William and Dorothy Wordsworth 1799-1808

A white 17th-18th century cottage once home to William and Dorothy Wordsworth between 1799-1808, and Mary Wordsworth from 1802. The front windows have been enlarged but the house is otherwise preserved largely as the Wordsworths left it. End entry by the stack under a little porch (of 1939), and straight into a small, crudely panelled parlour with an iron range and black flag floor. A bedroom and kitchen complete the downstairs, the sitting room is located upstairs over the parlour.(5115) Tree ring dating of the cottage timbers was carried out by the Nottingham Tree-Ring Dating Laboratory in 2010. 17 samples were taken but only ten were viable for dating. These samples did not match and did not date independently and remain undated providing no independent dating evidence for the chronological development of the house. (S5114). Also mentioned in the C&WAAS 2011 transactions (S5202).
